Cloke
KLOHK
noun
The Authorized Version’s spelling of cloak, through Old French cloque, a bell — so named from the shape of the wide outer garment hanging bell-like from the shoulders; hence also the figure of anything spread over to hide what is beneath.

Biblical Definition

The cloke is the wide outer garment worn over the coat, the last covering a man had and often his bedding by night, which is why the law forbade keeping a poor man’s pledged garment past sundown. Our Lord takes it up in the Sermon on the Mount: “if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also” (Mat 5:40). The command is not that we care nothing for justice, but that a disciple will sooner be stripped than be litigious, and will not clutch the last covering when peace with a brother is the price. Paul, at the end of his life and cold in a Roman cell, sends for the cloke he left at Troas with Carpus (2Ti 4:13) — a plain reminder that the apostle who wrote of the third heaven still needed a coat in winter. But the word’s second use is the sharper one. A cloke covers, and therefore Scripture names it as the very figure of pretence: Christ says of those who heard Him and rejected Him, “now they have no cloke for their sin” (Joh 15:22); Paul denies ever using flattering words “as a cloke of covetousness” (1Th 2:5); and Peter warns the free man not to use his liberty “for a cloke of maliciousness” (1Pe 2:16). The garment men throw over sin is always someone else’s virtue.

Webster 1828 Definition

A loose outer garment worn over the rest; hence, figuratively, any covering or pretext thrown over sin to hide it.

expand to see more

CLOKE, n. [Old Fr. cloque, a bell, from the shape.] A loose outer garment worn over the other clothes, covering the whole person.

Hence, a cover; a pretext; a pretence; that which conceals a design or a fault.

In the law, the outer garment taken in pledge must be restored before sundown, being the poor man’s covering by night (Exo 22:26-27).

Christ commands the disciple sued for his coat to yield the cloke also (Mat 5:40; Luk 6:29).

Figurative in Joh 15:22, 1Th 2:5, and 1Pe 2:16 — a cloke for sin, for covetousness, for maliciousness.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:40 — "And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also."

Joh 15:22 — "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin."

1Pe 2:16 — "As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God."

2Ti 4:13 — "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments."

Modern Corruption

The cloke is alive and thriving. What has changed is its fabric: sin is now covered with explanation — circumstance, upbringing, temperament, brain chemistry — and confession is treated as the unhealthy thing to be talked out of.

expand to see more

Christ’s verdict in Joh 15:22 is that light removes the covering: once He had come and spoken, the sin stood naked and no cloke could be found for it. Our age has answered by weaving new ones. The besetting sin is renamed a condition, the temper a wiring, the appetite an orientation, the cruelty a wound passed down; each account may hold some measure of truth about the occasion of the sin, and each becomes a cloke the moment it is offered in the place of confession. Scripture does not deny that men are shaped by what befalls them — it speaks constantly of the fathers’ sins, of affliction, of the frame that God remembers to be dust — but it never permits the shaping to become the excuse. David had every circumstance to plead and pleaded none of them: “against thee, thee only, have I sinned.” The reason is mercy, not severity. Nothing that is cloked can be forgiven, because nothing that is cloked is confessed, and “he that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).

Peter names the most refined cloke of all: liberty. “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness” — that is, taking the true doctrine that a Christian is free from the law’s condemnation and pulling it over conduct the law condemns. Paul’s version is flattery serving greed. In both cases the covering is not a lie but a truth misapplied, which is what makes it hard to strip off; the man is quoting sound doctrine while doing wickedness. The remedy is the one Christ Himself supplies. He does not merely tear the cloke away; He offers another garment in its place, the best robe brought out for the returning son. Confession is safe precisely because there is a covering that God Himself gives, and no man ever had to invent his own who was willing to wear Christ’s.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The wide outer garment — a poor man’s last covering, and Scripture’s standing figure for the pretext thrown over sin.

expand to see more

Cloke — the Authorized Version’s spelling of cloak; Old French cloque, a bell, from the garment’s shape.

Greek himation in Mat 5:40, the outer garment as against the chiton or coat.

Greek prophasis in Joh 15:22, 1Th 2:5, 1Pe 2:16 — a pretext, a thing put forward to cover.

Greek phelones in 2Ti 4:13, a traveller’s heavy cape left behind at Troas.

Isa 59:17 clothes the LORD Himself with zeal as a cloke — the one covering that hides nothing.

Usage

"Yield the cloke rather than the peace: Mat 5:40 puts a brother above the last garment you own."

"A cloke for sin is usually a truth misapplied — liberty, providence, temperament — which is what makes it stick."

"Nothing cloked is confessed, and nothing unconfessed is forgiven; Pro 28:13 makes uncovering the way to mercy."
